claim: The Notch pathway leads to gene activation when ligand and receptor engage upon cell contact.
source: Notch is a key signalling pathway that leads to gene activation when ligand and receptor engage upon cell contact (Bray, 2016; Kopan, 2012; Borggrefe and Oswald, 2009).
evidence: Supported by multiple citations to established literature on Notch signaling

claim: Physical interaction between ligand and receptor brings about a conformational change that permits proteolytic cleavage and release of Notch intracellular domain (NICD).
source: The physical interaction brings about a conformational change that permits proteolytic cleavage and release of Notch intracellular domain (NICD) (Kovall et al., 2017; Kopan and Ilagan, 2009; Sprinzak and Blacklow, 2021).
evidence: Supported by citations to literature describing the molecular mechanism of Notch activation

claim: NICD forms a complex with CSL and Mastermind (Mam), a coactivator.
source: This moiety forms a complex with CSL (CBF-1/RBPJ-κ in mammals, Suppressor of Hairless in Drosophila and LAG-1 in Caenorhabditis elegans), a transcription factor that binds to specific DNA motifs, and Mastermind (Mam), a coactivator (; Nam et al., 2006; Wilson and Kovall, 2006).
evidence: Supported by citations to studies characterizing the tripartite complex

claim: The tripartite activation complex promotes transcription from target genes where it is recruited.
source: This tripartite activation complex promotes transcription from the target genes where it is recruited.
evidence: Based on established understanding of the Notch transcription complex function

claim: The sites of recruitment differ according to cellular context, resulting in different transcriptional outcomes.
source: The sites of recruitment differ according to the cellular context, resulting in different transcriptional outcomes and suggesting that other factors are important in preparing the targets for activation (Bray and Gomez-Lamarca, 2018).
evidence: Supported by citation to previous work on context-dependent Notch signaling

claim: Release of NICD brings about rapid and robust transcriptional responses within minutes.
source: In addition, release of NICD brings about rapid and robust transcriptional responses within minutes, raising the question how the molecules of cleaved Notch achieve this so efficiently (Boukhatmi et al., 2020; Housden et al., 2013; Ilagan et al., 2011).
evidence: Supported by citations to studies documenting rapid transcriptional responses

claim: Sequence-specific transcription factors, key co-activators, and RNA polymerase II undergo dynamic clustering within a nucleus.
source: Many different studies report that sequence-specific transcription factors, key co-activators, and RNA polymerase II (Pol II) itself undergo dynamic clustering within a nucleus (Cho et al., 2022; Sabari et al., 2018; Cho et al., 2018; Rippe and Papantonis, 2022).
evidence: Supported by multiple citations to studies on transcription factor clustering

claim: Clustering is mediated by a combination of specific structure-mediated interactions and multivalent interactions among intrinsically disordered regions (IDRs).
source: Clustering appears to be mediated by a combination of specific structure-mediated interactions (e.g. DNA-binding, protein–protein interactions) and multivalent interactions among intrinsically disordered regions (IDRs) present in most transcription factors (Brodsky et al., 2020; Trojanowski et al., 2022).
evidence: Supported by citations to studies on mechanisms of transcription factor clustering

claim: All members of the Notch activator complex contain unstructured regions that could contribute to the assembly of a hub.
source: Indeed, all members of the Notch activator complex contain unstructured regions that could contribute to the assembly of a hub.
evidence: Based on inference from known protein structures and the context of transcription hub formation

claim: The N-terminal region of Mam proteins contains a conserved helix responsible for direct interactions with CSL and NICD.
source: The formation of the tripartite Notch activator complex involves a conserved helix in the N-terminal region of Mam proteins which is responsible for the direct interactions with CSL and NICD (Nam et al., 2006; Wilson and Kovall, 2006).
evidence: Supported by citations to structural studies of the Notch complex

claim: The remainder of Mam proteins are poorly conserved and appear to be predominantly unstructured.
source: The remainder of the large Mam proteins are poorly conserved and appear to be predominantly unstructured albeit to have potential roles in recruiting other cofactors (Kitagawa, 2016; Just Ribeiro and Wallberg, 2009).
evidence: Supported by citations to studies on Mam protein structure and function

claim: Human MAML1 interacts with the histone acetyl transferase CBP/p300.
source: For example, there is evidence that human MAML1 interacts with the histone acetyl transferase CBP/p300, which is present at Notch-regulated enhancers in genome-wide studies (Just Ribeiro and Wallberg, 2009; Baghdadi et al., 2018; Castel et al., 2013), and whose recruitment is implicated in activating some targets (Rogers et al., 2020; Fryer et al., 2002).
evidence: Supported by multiple citations to studies on MAML1-CBP/p300 interactions

claim: The C-terminal portion of MAML1 is suggested to recruit CDK8, the enzymatic core of the Mediator kinase module.
source: The C-terminal portion of MAML1 is also suggested to recruit CDK8, the enzymatic core of the Mediator kinase module (Fryer et al., 2004; Janody and Treisman, 2011; Wallberg et al., 2002).
evidence: Supported by citations to studies on MAML1-CDK8 interactions

claim: CSL is recruited in a very dynamic manner to a target genomic locus in vivo.
source: Using this strategy, we have previously shown that CSL is recruited in a very dynamic manner to a target genomic locus in vivo (Gomez-Lamarca et al., 2018).
evidence: Supported by citation to previous work by the authors

claim: CSL exists in both co-repressor and co-activator complexes.
source: However, as CSL exists in both co-repressor and co-activator complexes (Franz and Kovall, 2018), the extent that these dynamics reflect the characteristics of the activation complex remains to be established.
evidence: Supported by citation to literature on CSL complex composition

claim: GFP or Halo tags were inserted into the N-terminus of endogenous Mam using CRISPR-Cas9 genome editing.
source: To track Mam dynamic behaviours in vivo, we inserted GFP or Halo into the N-terminus of the endogenous Mam using CRISPR-Cas9 genome editing (Gomez-Lamarca et al., 2018).
evidence: Description of experimental method performed by the authors

claim: The resulting flies with tagged Mam are homozygous viable with no evident phenotypes, indicating that the tagged Mam proteins are fully functional.
source: The resulting flies are homozygous viable with no evident phenotypes, indicating that the tagged Mam proteins are fully functional.
evidence: Based on experimental observations of fly viability and phenotype

claim: Mam was robustly recruited to E(spl)-C in Notch ON conditions in a similar manner to CSL.
source: Comparing the localisation of GFP::Mam in Notch OFF and Notch ON conditions, it was immediately evident that Mam was robustly recruited to E(spl)-C in Notch ON conditions in a similar manner to CSL (Gomez-Lamarca et al., 2018).
evidence: Based on live imaging data comparing Notch OFF and ON conditions

claim: In Notch OFF conditions, both CSL and Mam were diffuse throughout the nucleus, with a low level of CSL, but not Mam, present at E(spl)-C.
source: In Notch OFF conditions, both proteins were diffuse throughout the nucleus, with a low level of CSL, but not Mam, present at E(spl)-C.
evidence: Based on live imaging observations in Notch OFF conditions

claim: In Notch ON conditions, strong enrichment of both Mam and CSL was consistently detected around E(spl)-C, where the two proteins co-localise in a correlated manner.
source: In Notch ON conditions, strong enrichment of both Mam and CSL was consistently detected around E(spl)-C, where the two proteins co-localise in a correlated manner (Figure 1B, Figure 1—figure supplement 1C).
evidence: Based on live imaging data and correlation analysis shown in figures

claim: CSL had a rapid recovery (t1/2 = 9 s) in FRAP experiments at E(spl)-C in Notch ON conditions.
source: Unlike CSL, which had a rapid recovery (t1/2 = 9 s), Mam exhibited slower dynamics (t1/2 = 40 s) and failed to fully recover over the time course of the experiment (Figure 1C).
evidence: Based on FRAP experimental measurements shown in Figure 1C

claim: Mam exhibited slower dynamics (t1/2 = 40 s) and failed to fully recover over the time course of the FRAP experiment.
source: Unlike CSL, which had a rapid recovery (t1/2 = 9 s), Mam exhibited slower dynamics (t1/2 = 40 s) and failed to fully recover over the time course of the experiment (Figure 1C).
evidence: Based on FRAP experimental measurements shown in Figure 1C

claim: The Mam-containing activation complexes have different properties from the majority of CSL complexes.
source: The results therefore suggest that the Mam-containing activation complexes have different properties from the majority of CSL complexes.
evidence: Inference drawn from the FRAP recovery differences between Mam and CSL

claim: Hairless has a fast recovery in FRAP experiments, with a profile close to that of CSL.
source: In FRAP experiments, Hairless has a fast recovery, with a profile close to that of CSL (Figure 1C), consistent with a significant fraction of CSL being complexed with Hairless even in Notch ON conditions (Gomez-Lamarca et al., 2018).
evidence: Based on FRAP experimental data shown in Figure 1C

claim: A significant fraction of CSL is complexed with Hairless even in Notch ON conditions.
source: In FRAP experiments, Hairless has a fast recovery, with a profile close to that of CSL (Figure 1C), consistent with a significant fraction of CSL being complexed with Hairless even in Notch ON conditions (Gomez-Lamarca et al., 2018).
evidence: Inference from FRAP data and supported by citation to previous work

claim: Hairless depletion by RNAi reduced CSL levels and recruitment and slowed its FRAP recovery.
source: In contrast, CSL levels and recruitment were reduced and its FRAP recovery was slowed, albeit not to the extent that it recapitulated the Mam profile (Figure 1C', Figure 1—figure supplement 1E).
evidence: Based on FRAP and imaging experiments with Hairless RNAi shown in figures

claim: Mam recruitment levels and dynamics measured by FRAP were unchanged by Hairless depletion.
source: As expected, Mam recruitment levels and the dynamics measured by FRAP were unchanged (Figure 1C', Figure 1—figure supplement 1E ).
evidence: Based on FRAP experiments with Hairless RNAi shown in figures

claim: The activation complexes, containing CSL and Mam, have slower dynamics than the repressor complexes, containing CSL and Hairless.
source: Together, the results indicate that the activation complexes, containing CSL and Mam, have slower dynamics than the repressor complexes, containing CSL and Hairless, and that the recovery of CSL reflects its participation in the two types of complexes.
evidence: Conclusion drawn from FRAP experiments comparing different complexes

claim: A greater proportion (55%) of Mam complexes were in the bound state than CSL complexes (39%).
source: A greater proportion (55%) of Mam complexes were in the bound state than CSL complexes (39%), consistent with the differences between their FRAP curves (Figure 1—figure supplement 1F).
evidence: Based on single-particle tracking analysis shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1F

claim: Both CSL and Mam trajectories were significantly enriched in a region of approximately 0.5 µm around the target locus in Notch ON conditions.
source: In comparison to their average distribution across the nucleus, both CSL and Mam trajectories were significantly enriched in a region of approximately 0.5 µm around the target locus in Notch ON conditions, reflecting robust Notch-dependent recruitment to this gene complex (Figure 1D).
evidence: Based on single-particle tracking trajectory density analysis shown in Figure 1D

claim: Mam trajectories had the longest durations (up to 15 s), Hairless trajectories were the shortest (up to 5–7 s), and CSL trajectories were intermediate (up to 10 s).
source: There were clear differences between the trajectory durations for Mam, CSL, and Hairless. Mam trajectories had the longest durations (up to 15 s), Hairless trajectories were the shortest (up to 5–7 s), and CSL trajectories were intermediate (up to 10 s) (Figure 1E).
evidence: Based on single-particle tracking trajectory duration analysis shown in Figure 1E

claim: Mam-containing complexes have on average longer residence times than other CSL complexes.
source: These data confirm that Mam-containing complexes have on average longer residence times than other CSL complexes which, together with the higher proportion of bound molecules overall, explains the slower recovery dynamics measured by FRAP.
evidence: Conclusion drawn from trajectory duration analysis and FRAP data

claim: Once recruited, Mam can be retained at target loci independently of CSL by interactions with other factors so that it resides for longer.
source: It is, therefore, possible that, once recruited, Mam can be retained at target loci independently of CSL by interactions with other factors so that it resides for longer.
evidence: Speculation based on the observation that Mam has longer trajectories than expected from CSL dynamics alone

claim: The diffuse enrichment of CSL and Mam at E(spl)-C was not maintained when tissues were fixed.
source: However, the diffuse enrichment was not maintained when the tissues were fixed, a characteristic reported for proteins present in condensate-like hubs (Irgen-Gioro et al., 2022; Figure 2—figure supplement 1A).
evidence: Based on comparison of live and fixed imaging shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1A

claim: The amounts of CSL recruited to loci with 12 and 48 ectopic CSL binding sites were almost identical.
source: Remarkably the amounts of CSL recruited to loci with 12 and 48 ectopic sites were almost identical.
evidence: Based on imaging experiments comparing recruitment to different numbers of binding sites

claim: There is not a direct correlation between the number of CSL binding motifs and the amount of CSL recruited under Notch ON conditions.
source: Thus, there is not a direct correlation between the number of motifs and the amount of CSL recruited under these conditions, although we note that DNA binding is a prerequisite as no recruitment occurs with CSL mutant that lacks DNA binding (Gomez-Lamarca et al., 2018).
evidence: Conclusion drawn from experiments with different numbers of binding sites

claim: There was no decrease in recruitment at the endogenous E(spl)-C locus, even in nuclei with a 48 CSL-motif insertion.
source: Nor does it appear that the amounts of CSL complexes are a limiting factor as there was no decrease in recruitment at the endogenous E(spl)-C locus, even in nuclei with a 48 CSL-motif insertion.
evidence: Based on imaging experiments with ectopic binding sites

claim: The C-terminal region from NICD was the most strongly enriched at E(spl)-C in Notch ON conditions among the IDRs tested.
source: Of the IDRs tested, the C-terminal region from NICD was the most strongly enriched at E(spl)-C in Notch ON conditions.
evidence: Based on imaging experiments with IDR-GFP fusions

claim: A low level of enrichment was evident for a shorter NICD fragment lacking the C-terminal PEST sequences and for Med1 IDR.
source: A low level of enrichment was also evident for a shorter NICD fragment, which lacked the C-terminal PEST sequences and for Med 1 IDR but not for the terminal regions of CSL.
evidence: Based on imaging experiments with IDR-GFP fusions

claim: Little or no enrichment occurred with Mam-IDRs at E(spl)-C.
source: Surprisingly, little or no enrichment occurred with Mam-IDRs, despite this large protein being reported to interact with p300 and other factors (Figure 2—figure supplement 1C) and the mammalian MamL1 forming puncta when overexpressed (Wu et al., 2000).
evidence: Based on imaging experiments with Mam-IDR-GFP fusions shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1C

claim: Mam-nIDR::GFP fusion was present in droplets, suggesting that it can self-associate when present in a high local concentration.
source: Notably, however, Mam-nIDR::GFP fusion was present in droplets, suggesting that it can self-associate when present in a high local concentration (Figure 2—figure supplement 1B; Banani et al., 2017).
evidence: Based on imaging observations shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1B

claim: The IDR in NICD may contribute to the localised enrichments at target loci in Notch ON cells.
source: Our results, therefore, suggest that the IDR in NICD may contribute to the localised enrichments at target loci in Notch ON cells, potentially in combination with IDRs present in other recruited factors.
evidence: Inference drawn from IDR enrichment experiments

claim: Deletion of the IDR from NICD led to a reduction in the levels and stability of Mam recruitment to E(spl)-C.
source: In support of this hypothesis, deletion of the IDR from NICD led to a reduction in the levels and stability of Mam recruitment to E(spl)-C (Figure 2D).
evidence: Based on imaging experiments with NICD lacking IDR shown in Figure 2D

claim: There is an enrichment for slow-diffusing and a depletion of fast-moving particles close to the E(spl)-C locus, with these altered properties extending to a region of up to 1 μm away.
source: The results show that there is an enrichment for slow-diffusing and a depletion of fast-moving particles close to the locus, with these altered properties extending to a region of up to 1 μm away (Figure 2E).
evidence: Based on spatial analysis of single-particle tracking data shown in Figure 2E

claim: CSL-Mam complexes are recruited and form a hub of high protein concentrations around the target locus in Notch ON conditions.
source: Together, our data support the model that CSL-Mam complexes are recruited and form a hub of high protein concentrations around the target locus in Notch ON conditions and suggest that IDR interactions, as well as DNA binding, contribute to their recruitment and retention in a region surrounding the active enhancers.
evidence: Conclusion drawn from multiple lines of experimental evidence including imaging, FRAP, and SPT

claim: Triptolide treatment did not change Mam enrichment or recovery at E(spl)-C.
source: No change in Mam enrichment or recovery was detected, arguing that Mam recruitment is not dependent on initiation or RNA production (Figure 3A and B).
evidence: Based on imaging and FRAP experiments with triptolide treatment shown in Figures 3A and B

claim: Mam recruitment is not dependent on transcription initiation or RNA production.
source: No change in Mam enrichment or recovery was detected, arguing that Mam recruitment is not dependent on initiation or RNA production (Figure 3A and B).
evidence: Conclusion drawn from triptolide treatment experiments

claim: A485 treatment for 1 hr severely reduced the levels of H3K27Ac and E(spl)m3 transcription.
source: Tissues were exposed to A485 for 1 hr which was sufficient to severely reduce the levels of H3K27Ac and E(spl)m3 transcription, indicating that the treatment was effective (Figure 3—figure supplement 1B and C).
evidence: Based on immunofluorescence and smFISH experiments shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 1B and C

claim: There was no change in the recruitment of Mam following CBP inhibition with A485.
source: Surprisingly, however, there was no change in the recruitment of Mam in these conditions (Figure 3C).
evidence: Based on imaging experiments with A485 treatment shown in Figure 3C

claim: CBP depletion by RNAi did not change Mam recruitment.
source: We also depleted CBP by RNAi and, as with the drug treatment, Mam recruitment was unchanged (Figure 3D, Figure 3—figure supplement 1J).
evidence: Based on imaging experiments with CBP RNAi shown in Figure 3D

claim: CBP is not essential for the recruitment of Mam complexes to the hub formed at the E(spl)-C locus.
source: Based on these results, we conclude that CBP is not essential for the recruitment of Mam complexes to the hub formed at the E(spl)-C locus.
evidence: Conclusion drawn from CBP inhibition and depletion experiments

claim: Med13 depletion led to a loss of E(spl)m3 transcription.
source: Med13 depletion led to a loss of E(spl)m3 transcription, confirming its role (Figure 3—figure supplement 1E).
evidence: Based on smFISH experiments with Med13 RNAi shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 1E

claim: Med13 depletion led to a substantial reduction in Mam recruitment to E(spl)-C in Notch ON cells.
source: In these conditions, we detected a substantial reduction in Mam recruitment to E(spl)-C in Notch ON cells, suggesting that the CDK module plays a role in retaining Mam at target sites (Figure 3E and G).
evidence: Based on imaging experiments with Med13 RNAi shown in Figures 3E and G

claim: Senexin B and Senexin A treatment significantly impaired Mam levels at E(spl)-C.
source: In both cases, the treatment was sufficient to significantly impair Mam levels at E(spl)-C (Figure 3F, Figure 3—figure supplement 1D) while a CDK9 inhibitor, NVP2, had no effect on the same assays despite a loss of E(spl)m3 transcription (Figure 3—figure supplement 1H and I).
evidence: Based on imaging experiments with Senexin treatment shown in Figure 3F and Figure 3—figure supplement 1D

claim: CDK9 inhibitor NVP2 had no effect on Mam recruitment despite a loss of E(spl)m3 transcription.
source: In both cases, the treatment was sufficient to significantly impair Mam levels at E(spl)-C (Figure 3F, Figure 3—figure supplement 1D) while a CDK9 inhibitor, NVP2, had no effect on the same assays despite a loss of E(spl)m3 transcription (Figure 3—figure supplement 1H and I).
evidence: Based on imaging and smFISH experiments with NVP2 treatment shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 1H and I

claim: Significant enrichment of Med13::YFP was detected at E(spl)-C in Notch ON nuclei.
source: Significant enrichment of Med13::YFP was detected at E(spl)-C in Notch ON nuclei (Figure 3H), demonstrating that it is present in the hub with Mam.
evidence: Based on imaging experiments with Med13::YFP shown in Figure 3H

claim: Neither depletion of Med13 nor Senexin treatments caused any significant reduction in the levels of CSL recruited.
source: Despite their effects on Mam recruitment, neither depletion of Med13 nor Senexin treatments caused any significant reduction in the levels of CSL recruited. On the contrary, a small increase occurred (Figure 3E and F).
evidence: Based on imaging experiments with Med13 RNAi and Senexin treatment shown in Figures 3E and F

claim: CSL-H[mut] is not enriched at E(spl)-C in Senexin-treated tissues.
source: This retains normal recruitment in control Notch ON conditions (Figure 3—figure supplement 1G), but, strikingly, it is not enriched at E(spl)-C in Senexin-treated tissues.
evidence: Based on imaging experiments with CSL-H[mut] and Senexin treatment shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 1G

claim: CSL requires Hairless interaction for its recruitment to E(spl)-C upon CDK8 inhibition.
source: This result suggests that CSL requires Hairless interaction for its recruitment to E(spl)-C upon CDK8 inhibition.
evidence: Inference drawn from experiments with CSL-H[mut] and Senexin treatment

claim: The CDK module is specifically involved in retaining Mam in the hub.
source: The differences in the effects on Mam and CSL imply that the CDK module is specifically involved in retaining Mam in the hub, and that in its absence other CSL complexes containing Hairless 'win-out' either because the altered conditions favour them and/or because they are the more abundant.
evidence: Conclusion drawn from differential effects of CDK module perturbation on Mam versus CSL

claim: MamDN expression in Notch ON conditions prevented recruitment of full-length Mam to E(spl)-C.
source: As predicted, MamDN expression in Notch ON conditions prevented recruitment of full-length Mam to E(spl)-C (Figure 4A).
evidence: Based on imaging experiments with MamDN expression shown in Figure 4A

claim: Nascent transcripts of E(spl)m3 were at very reduced levels in nuclei co-expressing MamDN.
source: Nascent transcripts of E(spl)m3 were detected at E(spl)-C in Notch ON nuclei and were at very reduced levels in nuclei co-expressing MamDN (Figure 4D and D'), confirming that target-gene transcription is blocked.
evidence: Based on smFISH experiments with MamDN expression shown in Figures 4D and D'

claim: Recruitment of CSL was unaffected by MamDN expression.
source: By contrast, recruitment of CSL was unaffected by MamDN expression. It was robustly recruited to E(spl)-C at a similar level to untreated Notch ON nuclei despite the absence of full-length Mam (Figure 4A'; Gomez-Lamarca et al., 2018).
evidence: Based on imaging experiments with MamDN expression shown in Figure 4A'

claim: The enrichment of Med13 was lost in the presence of MamDN.
source: In contrast to CSL, the enrichment of Med13 was lost in the presence of MamDN, revealing that Med13 recruitment requires Mam, as well as the converse (Figure 4C).
evidence: Based on imaging experiments with Med13::YFP and MamDN shown in Figure 4C

claim: Both E(spl)mβ and E(spl)m3 regulatory regions significantly increased in accessibility in Notch ON nuclei, which was maintained in the presence of MamDN.
source: Both regions significantly increased in accessibility in Notch ON nuclei which was maintained in the presence of MamDN (Figure 4B).
evidence: Based on ATAC-qPCR experiments shown in Figure 4B

claim: The levels of GFP::NICD-IDR recruited to E(spl)-C were similar in the presence and absence of MamDN.
source: In addition, we found that the levels of GFP::NICD-IDR recruited to E(spl)-C were similar in the presence and absence of MamDN (Figure 4—figure supplement 1B), arguing that a modified hub is still formed.
evidence: Based on imaging experiments with NICD-IDR and MamDN shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 1B

claim: The increased chromatin accessibility elicited by Notch activation can occur independently of Mam.
source: Altogether these observations support the model that the increased chromatin accessibility elicited by Notch activation can occur independently of Mam and must rely on other functions conferred by CSL and NICD (Gomez-Lamarca et al., 2018), while Mam is essential to recruit the Mediator CDK module and enable transcription.
evidence: Conclusion drawn from experiments with MamDN showing maintained accessibility but lost transcription

claim: Mam is essential to recruit the Mediator CDK module and enable transcription.
source: Altogether these observations support the model that the increased chromatin accessibility elicited by Notch activation can occur independently of Mam and must rely on other functions conferred by CSL and NICD (Gomez-Lamarca et al., 2018), while Mam is essential to recruit the Mediator CDK module and enable transcription.
evidence: Conclusion drawn from experiments showing loss of Med13 and transcription with MamDN

claim: CSL remained relatively constant through 4 hr and 8 hr time points after Notch switch-off while Mam levels at E(spl)-C decreased sharply after 4 hr.
source: Imaging Mam::GFP and CSL::mCherry simultaneously, it was evident that Mam recruitment levels decreased more rapidly. CSL remained relatively constant through both time points while, in contrast, the levels of Mam at E(spl)-C decreased sharply after 4 hr (Figure 5A).
evidence: Based on time-course imaging experiments after Notch withdrawal shown in Figure 5A

claim: After Notch activity decays, the locus remains accessible because when Mam-containing complexes are lost they are replaced by other CSL complexes.
source: Based on these results, we propose that, after Notch activity decays, the locus remains accessible because when Mam-containing complexes are lost they are replaced by other CSL complexes (e.g. co-repressor complexes).
evidence: Inference drawn from time-course experiments showing differential decay of Mam versus CSL

claim: Neither E(spl)mβ nor E(spl)m3 enhancer exhibited any reduction in accessibility at 8 hr after Notch withdrawal.
source: Neither enhancer exhibited any reduction in accessibility at this time point, consistent with the continued recruitment of CSL and the results obtained with MamDN (Figure 5B).
evidence: Based on ATAC-qPCR experiments after Notch withdrawal shown in Figure 5B

claim: Expression of E(spl)m3 was already significantly reduced at 4 hr after Notch withdrawal when levels of nascent transcripts at E(spl)-C and of cytoplasmic transcripts had both decreased.
source: In contrast, the gradual loss of Mam complexes was accompanied by reduced transcription, as detected by smFISH. Expression of E(spl)m3 was already significantly reduced at 4 hr when levels of nascent transcripts at E(spl)-C and of cytoplasmic transcripts had both decreased (Figure 5—figure supplement 1A).
evidence: Based on smFISH experiments after Notch withdrawal shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 1A

claim: By 8 hr after Notch withdrawal, both nascent and cytoplasmic E(spl)m3 transcripts were almost undetectable.
source: By 8 hr both nascent and cytoplasmic E(spl)m3 transcripts were almost undetectable (Figure 5—figure supplement 1A).
evidence: Based on smFISH experiments after Notch withdrawal shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 1A

claim: Strong CSL enrichment was detected 24 hr after transfer to the non-permissive temperature when there was no detectable transcription of E(spl)m3.
source: Indeed, we were still able to detect a strong CSL enrichment 24 hr after transfer to the non-permissive temperature at time when, consistent with shorter OFF periods, there was no detectable transcription of E(spl)m3 (Figure 5C).
evidence: Based on imaging and smFISH experiments 24 hr after Notch withdrawal shown in Figure 5C

claim: Cells that had been preactivated showed higher levels of E(spl)m3 transcription after 30 min in blue light compared to naïve cells.
source: Strikingly, after 30 min in blue light to activate Notch, cells that had been preactivated showed higher levels of E(spl)m3 transcription compared to naïve cells, indicating that the previous Notch exposure renders them more sensitive (Figure 5E and F).
evidence: Based on smFISH experiments with optogenetic Notch activation shown in Figures 5E and F

claim: Recruitment of Mam occurred more rapidly in preactivated cells in comparison to naïve cells.
source: During the subsequent activation and imaging, recruitment of Mam occurred more rapidly in preactivated cells in comparison to naïve cells, suggesting that the former are primed to rapidly reform an active hub containing Mam (Figure 5I).
evidence: Based on live imaging experiments tracking Mam recruitment shown in Figure 5I

claim: CSL recruitment and increased chromatin accessibility persist after Notch removal and after the loss of Mam-containing activation complexes.
source: Together, our data indicate that CSL recruitment and increased chromatin accessibility persist after Notch removal and after the loss of Mam-containing activation complexes.
evidence: Conclusion drawn from time-course experiments after Notch withdrawal

claim: Persistent CSL confers a memory state that enables re-assembly of an activation hub and more rapid initiation of transcription in response to subsequent Notch activity.
source: This persistent CSL confers a memory state that enables re-assembly of an activation hub and more rapid initiation of transcription in response to subsequent Notch activity.
evidence: Conclusion drawn from experiments showing enhanced response in preactivated cells

claim: Rbp3 enrichment at E(spl)-C in Notch ON cells was highly variable, with robust enrichment detected in a subset of nuclei but little/no enrichment in other cases.
source: When scanning all nuclei, it was evident that Rbp3 enrichment at E(spl)-C in Notch ON cells was highly variable. Robust enrichment was detected in a subset of nuclei, but, in other cases, there was little/no enrichment above nuclear levels (Figure 6—figure supplement 1B).
evidence: Based on imaging experiments with GFP::Rbp3 shown in Figure 6—figure supplement 1B

claim: 36% of Notch ON nuclei had significant Pol II enrichment and 64% had similar levels to Notch OFF.
source: Performing a Gaussian population fitting on the data, two populations gave the best fit and, based on these, 36% of nuclei had significant enrichment and 64% had similar levels to Notch OFF (Figure 6B, Figure 6—figure supplement 1B).
evidence: Based on Gaussian fitting analysis of Rbp3 enrichment data shown in Figure 6B

claim: Over 90% of Notch ON nuclei have significant Mam enrichment at E(spl)-C.
source: This differs from Mam where all nuclei fall into a single population that has significant Mam enrichment at E(spl)-C (Figure 6A, Figure 6—figure supplement 1A).
evidence: Based on Gaussian fitting analysis of Mam enrichment data shown in Figure 6A

claim: There is a limiting step which results in transcription initiation being probabilistic/stochastic in Notch ON conditions.
source: The striking difference in the proportions of nuclei with Pol II and with Mam enrichment implies that there is a limiting step, which results in transcription initiation being probabilistic/stochastic in these conditions.
evidence: Inference drawn from the discrepancy between Mam and Pol II enrichment proportions

claim: GFP::Med1 became enriched at E(spl)-C with a similar probability to Rbp3.
source: Using this endogenously tagged protein, which is homozygous viable, we found that GFP::Med1 became enriched at E(spl)-C with a similar probability to Rbp3 (Figure 6C).
evidence: Based on imaging experiments with GFP::Med1 shown in Figure 6C

claim: There was a significant correlation (R2 = 0.69) between Pol II and Med1 enrichment in Notch ON nuclei.
source: Indeed when we compared directly the enrichment of Pol II and Med1 in Notch ON nuclei, by using mCherry::Rbp1 (Cho et al., 2022) to monitor Pol II, we observed a significant correlation between the two proteins (R2 = 0.69, Figure 6E).
evidence: Based on correlation analysis of Med1 and Rbp1 enrichment shown in Figure 6E

claim: A robust band of MCP/MS2 nascent transcription at E(spl)-C was present in only 37% of Notch ON nuclei.
source: A robust band of MCP/MS2 nascent transcription at E(spl)-C was detected in Notch ON conditions, demonstrating that some nuclei were actively transcribing (Figure 6D, Figure 6—figure supplement 1D). However, this was present in only a third (37%) of nuclei.
evidence: Based on live imaging of MS2/MCP transcription shown in Figure 6D

claim: The proportion of active nuclei is similar to that with recruitment of Pol II and Med1.
source: These data show that only a subset of nuclei engage in active transcription, and that the proportion of active nuclei is similar to that with recruitment of Pol II and Med1.
evidence: Comparison of proportions from MS2/MCP, Pol II, and Med1 enrichment data

claim: The presence of Mam complexes is not sufficient to reliably drive all the steps required for transcription in every Notch ON nucleus.
source: These data demonstrate that the presence of Mam complexes is not sufficient to reliably drive all the steps required for transcription in every Notch ON nucleus. Instead, it appears that transcription is initiated stochastically.
evidence: Conclusion drawn from the observation that only ~1/3 of nuclei with Mam show active transcription

claim: The proportion of nuclei with MS2/MCP puncta increased dramatically to 70% following ecdysone treatment.
source: Strikingly, the proportion of active nuclei increased dramatically to 70% following ecdysone treatment. No such effects were seen in Notch OFF nuclei where E(spl)mβ remained silent even after ecdysone treatment (Figure 6F, Figure 6—figure supplement 1H).
evidence: Based on MS2/MCP imaging experiments with ecdysone treatment shown in Figure 6F

claim: The proportion of nuclei with clear enrichment of Pol II and Med1 was significantly increased by ecdysone treatment.
source: We further tested the effect of ecdysone by measuring changes in enrichment of Pol II and Med1 at E(spl)-C. The proportion of nuclei with clear enrichment of each factor was significantly increased (Figure 6F, Figure 6—figure supplement 1F and G).
evidence: Based on imaging experiments with ecdysone treatment shown in Figure 6F and supplements

claim: The switch from stochastic transcription elicited by Mam alone to more robust initiation with ecdysone correlated with the presence of Med1 and Pol II.
source: Thus, the switch from the more stochastic transcription elicited by recruitment of Mam alone to the more robust initiation when ecdysone was added, correlated with the presence of Med1 and Pol II.
evidence: Conclusion drawn from correlation between ecdysone treatment and Med1/Pol II recruitment

claim: Mediator recruitment may be what limits the probability of transcription.
source: As Mediator is reported to stabilise enhancer–promoter interactions, its recruitment may be what limits the probability of transcription (Richter et al., 2022; Luyties and Taatjes, 2022).
evidence: Speculation based on known Mediator function and correlation with transcription probability

claim: In Notch ON nuclei, the activation complexes promote formation of a dynamic protein hub at a regulated gene locus that concentrates key factors including Mediator CDK module.
source: By tracking these complexes in real time, we unveiled three important features (Figure 7): (i) in Notch ON nuclei, the activation complexes promote formation of a dynamic protein hub at a regulated gene locus that concentrates key factors including Mediator CDK module
evidence: Summary conclusion from multiple experimental approaches shown throughout the manuscript

claim: The composition of the hub is changeable and the footprint persists after Notch withdrawal conferring a memory that enables rapid reactivation.
source: (ii) the composition of the hub is changeable and the footprint persists after Notch withdrawal conferring a memory that enables rapid reactivation
evidence: Summary conclusion from time-course and reactivation experiments

claim: Transcription is probabilistic in Notch ON nuclei, such that only a third of nuclei with a hub are actively transcribing.
source: (iii) transcription is probabilistic in Notch ON nuclei, such that only a third of nuclei with a hub are actively transcribing.

claim: Stochastic differences in Notch pathway output can arise downstream of receptor activation.
source: This has far-reaching implications because it reveals that stochastic differences in Notch pathway output can arise downstream of receptor activation.
